analysis.one_liner: Opens more federal waters off Florida, Alaska, and the Atlantic to oil and gas drilling and lifts the crude oil export ban.
analysis.headline: The Senate Energy Committee reported the bill to the floor on the day it was introduced in September 2015, but it never received a floor vote and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Interior Department to hold oil and gas lease sales in the Eastern Gulf of Mexico — shrinking the drilling buffer off Florida from 125 miles to 50 — and in the Arctic Beaufort, Chukchi, and Cook Inlet areas, plus the South Atlantic off Georgia, the Carolinas, and Virginia. It would have lifted the ban on exporting U.S. crude oil, delayed Obama-era blowout-preventer and Arctic drilling safety rules for at least 180 days pending a new review, waived Endangered Species Act consultation for certain marine mammal permits, repealed a Clean Air Act provision covering offshore sources off Florida, and limited environmental reviews for the new lease sales. In exchange, it would have sent shares of drilling royalties to Gulf, Atlantic, and Alaska state governments and created a Tribal Resilience Fund for Alaska Native communities.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies, who would gain access to millions of acres of newly mandated federal lease sales, longer 20-year lease terms in the Arctic, and delayed safety and air-pollution rules. Crude oil producers and exporters would gain from the lifting of the export ban. State governments in the Gulf, Alaska, and the South Atlantic would gain royalty shares for land conservation, transportation, and beach projects, and Alaska Native tribes would gain a new climate-resilience grant fund.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have directed 75% of certain Gulf drilling revenues to Gulf producing states (adding Florida), with 25% counted as income to the Land and Water Conservation Fund for state financial assistance.

It would have sent 37.5% of Atlantic drilling revenues to states adjacent to the South Atlantic planning area for land and water conservation, public transportation, clean energy, and beach nourishment.

It would have created a Tribal Resilience Fund with grants of up to $200 million per year to Indian tribes for climate adaptation, including relocating villages threatened by erosion and building evacuation infrastructure.
It would have banned drilling that conflicts with military operations and required consultation with affected governors before lease sales within 30 nautical miles of the coastline.

It would have funded university partnerships to study the Atlantic shelf's oil and gas potential, including one historically Black college or university per participating state, with preference for schools serving veterans.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers and the Treasury, who would keep a smaller share of drilling royalties. Coastal communities off Florida and the South Atlantic would bear new spill and industrialization risk from mandated nearby lease sales. Arctic ecosystems and Alaska Native subsistence communities would face new drilling pressure from required Beaufort and Chukchi sales, with marine mammal permitting fast-tracked and exempted from Endangered Species Act consultation. Offshore workers and coastal residents would also wait longer for stronger blowout-preventer and Arctic drilling safety rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have shrunk the drilling moratorium off Florida's coast from 125 miles to 50 miles and mandated three Eastern Gulf lease sales in 2018-2020, putting drilling within sight of Florida beaches and the tourism economy that depends on them.

It would have delayed the post-Deepwater Horizon blowout-preventer and well-control rule and the Arctic exploratory drilling rule by at least 180 days and required Interior to re-propose them after a new cost analysis, and it would have barred Arctic drilling rules for coastal residents' protection from a major well blowout.

It would have exempted marine mammal incidental-harassment authorizations from Endangered Species Act consultation and declared that any taking under such an authorization is not a prohibited taking, and it would have repealed the Clean Air Act requirement for offshore air pollution controls off Florida's Gulf Coast.
It would have stripped the environmental review for new lease sales of any nonleasing alternative, requiring Interior to analyze only the preferred leasing action and one alternative.

Lifting the crude oil export ban would have exposed independent refiners and shipbuilding yards to new competition; the bill itself required the GAO to study those effects on consumers and refiners rather than treating the outcome as settled.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The revenue-sharing, conservation funding, and tribal resilience provisions are real benefits, but they are attached to a package whose core is mandating drilling in areas where it is currently restricted — including within 50 miles of Florida and in Arctic waters — and weakening the safety, air-quality, endangered-species, and environmental-review protections that would apply. The benefits flow to a handful of state governments and tribes; the risks fall on coastal residents, Arctic ecosystems, and anyone whose air, water, or coastline depends on the rules being rolled back. The bill's own text acknowledges uncertainty about export-ban effects by ordering a GAO review of impacts on consumers and refiners.

outcome.mechanism: The Energy Committee reported it straight to the Senate calendar the day it was introduced, but no senator ever voted on it and it died when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced and reported to the Senate by the Energy and Natural Resources Committee as an original measure on September 9, 2015, with written report No. 114-137 and minority views filed, and was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 217).
The bill had zero cosponsors in the Senate.
No further action was taken; the bill remained on the calendar without a floor vote through the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never passed, offshore drillers and crude exporters did not get the mandated lease sales, delayed safety rules, or export authorization, the Treasury kept all offshore royalty revenue rather than sharing it out, and the marine mammal, air-quality, and safety-rule protections it would have waived or delayed stayed in effect. Coastal communities off Florida and the South Atlantic avoided the mandated nearby drilling.

sides.party_line_note: No Democrat cosponsored the bill and committee Democrats filed minority views; the bill was never voted on by the full Senate, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: The bill would have mandated lease sales in the Eastern Gulf, Arctic Beaufort, Chukchi, Cook Inlet, and South Atlantic, extended Arctic lease terms to 20 years, and delayed blowout-preventer and Arctic drilling safety rules. Its gains — new access to restricted federal waters with weakened oversight — come at the cost of spill, air, and wildlife risk borne by coastal and Arctic communities.

Section 501 would have ended the federal license requirement for exporting domestic crude oil, letting producers sell into higher-priced world markets. The bill's own findings concede the effects on consumers were projected rather than proven and require a GAO review of impacts on consumers, independent refiners, and shipyards.

Lifting the crude export ban would have exposed refiners to higher input costs and new competition; the bill directs the GAO to study job losses in shipbuilding and ship repair and adverse impacts on consumers and refiners rather than claiming they would not occur.

industries.industry: Alaska Native tribes and Arctic coastal villages
industries.note: The bill would have created a Tribal Resilience Fund with up to $200 million a year for climate adaptation, village relocation, and evacuation infrastructure, funded from a share of Alaska offshore revenues. This benefit is real, but it is financed by opening the Arctic waters adjacent to these communities to mandated drilling.

industries.industry: Gulf, Alaska, and Atlantic coastal state governments
industries.note: The bill would have directed substantial royalty shares to Gulf producing states (adding Florida), Alaska and its coastal subdivisions, and South Atlantic states for conservation, transportation, beaches, and clean energy. States gain only if drilling in the adjacent federal waters actually happens.
